name: Bodyweight Squat
description: A fundamental strength-building movement involving bending at the knees and hips and rising back up, improving daily functional tasks like getting up from a seated position. It engages quadriceps, hamstrings, glutes, adductors, and core muscles. 1
cues: Initiate by pushing glutes and hips backward before bending knees

name: Good Morning
description: A posteriorly top-loaded hip hinge exercise that primarily strengthens the lower back, hamstrings, and glutes, developing a strong posterior chain. It involves flexing at the hip while maintaining rigidity at the knees, similar to picking something up off the ground. 1
progressions: gradual bi-weekly increases); Zercher Good Mornings 9
cues: squeeze shoulder blades to create a "shelf" for the bar

name: Forward Lunge
description: A unilateral, bodyweight exercise that works muscles throughout the lower body by taking a large step forward and lowering until both legs are at nearly a 90-degree angle. It targets quadriceps, glutes, hamstrings, hip flexors, and adductors, while also increasing core stabilization. 18
regressions: Smaller steps forward (decrease range of motion/depth) 18
contraindications: Noticeable knee pain; knee extending beyond leading toes; rear knee resting on ground; leaning backward/forward or hyperextending neck 18
cues: engage core and keep back straight
drive through heel of front foot to return to standing 18

name: Push-up
description: A classic bodyweight exercise that works multiple muscle groups including the chest (pectorals), shoulders (deltoids, rotator cuff), and triceps, while engaging the core for stability. It involves pushing your body weight away from the floor. 1
cues: Hands slightly outside shoulder-width at chest level

name: Inverted Row
description: An effective bodyweight exercise to strengthen pulling muscles (back and biceps) by pulling the body toward a bar. The difficulty adjusts with body angle: more horizontal is harder, more upright is easier. It also engages midsection muscles for rigidity. 1
cues: pull through elbows to bring chest to bar

name: Russian Twist
description: A core exercise involving seated torso rotations, primarily engaging the obliques and stabilizing the core. It helps govern the body's ability to produce and resist rotational forces, crucial for sports and core stability. 2
contraindications: Lower back pain (if form is compromised)
cues: move slowly - it is a stability exercise (the slower you move, the more muscle will engage to help you balance) 5

name: Walking
description: The most foundational cyclical movement pattern used to move from one place to another. It is a low-impact cardio exercise vital for overall mobility and should be incorporated into warm-up and cool-down routines. 1

name: Barbell Back Squat
description: The barbell back squat is a highly regarded leg exercise, frequently positioned as a cornerstone in lower body training programs. Performed with a barbell resting on the upper traps in a squat rack, this multi-joint movement effectively recruits the largest and most powerful muscles in the body, including the quadriceps, hamstrings, and glutes, while also significantly engaging the core for stability. It places a particular emphasis on strengthening the posterior chain.27
progressions: Increasing the weight lifted is the primary progression. Deeper squat depth can also be pursued gradually as mobility and control improve.7
regressions: which helps build control and teaches hip engagement
which aids in maintaining an upright torso. The Barbell Front Squat can also serve as a regression for those needing less spinal loading than a back squat.7
contraindications: or poor foundational mobility should approach this exercise with caution or opt for regressions.7
cues: Key cues include "create tension on the bar" by squeezing it into the upper back, "keep your chest up" to prevent rounding, and "screw your feet into the floor" to engage glutes and prevent knee caving. Other effective cues are "drive knees out," "drive shoulders back up into the bar," "get your back tight," "break the knees, then go straight down," "press the big toe into the ground," and "squat like you're in a Smith machine" (straight up and down).11

name: Barbell Deadlift
description: The barbell deadlift is a near-full body exercise that primarily targets the posterior chain muscles, including the glutes, hamstrings, and lower back. It also significantly recruits various other muscle groups, such as the core and forearms, making it a highly efficient compound movement. This exercise involves lifting a loaded barbell from the floor to a standing position, contributing to improved posture and core stability by strengthening the muscles that support the spine.28
progressions: The primary progression involves gradually increasing the weight lifted
adhering to the principle of progressive overload. Variations such as the conventional deadlift and sumo deadlift can also serve as progressions or alternatives to target muscles differently.29
regressions: mastering the hip hinge movement is crucial before adding significant load. Starting with lighter weights is recommended. Romanian Deadlifts (RDLs) can also serve as a preparatory exercise for the full deadlift.29
contraindications: Common errors to avoid include rounding the spine
as these can increase the risk of injury.28
cues: Initiate the movement with feet hip to shoulder-width apart. Key cues involve "bracing the abs," maintaining a "flat back," keeping the "bar close to the shins," and "pushing into the floor to lift." The movement should involve "maintaining the head and torso angle" until the bar passes the knees, then "standing upright" by "driving the hips forward".28

name: Barbell Bench Press
description: The barbell bench press is a highly effective multi-joint exercise for developing upper body strength. It efficiently targets virtually all major upper-body muscle groups, including the pectorals (chest), deltoids (shoulders), and triceps (back of the arms). The exercise is performed lying on a flat bench, pressing a barbell upwards from the chest.31
progressions: Increasing the weight is the most common progression. Other variations include the paused bench press
and incline or decline bench presses to target different muscle fibers or ranges of motion.31
regressions: Alternatives for building strength before heavy benching include Dumbbell Bench Press and Push-ups.8
contraindications: Common mistakes to avoid include excessive wrist flexion
a loose grip on the bar
performing the lift with a flat back (lack of arch)
as these can lead to increased stress and potential injury to the wrists
cues: Essential cues include keeping the "feet planted" for stability and leg drive, maintaining a "slight arch in the lower back," positioning the "eyes slightly behind the bar" for proper path, and actively "bending the bar" to promote external shoulder rotation. Other cues involve "pinching the glutes," "pinching and bringing down shoulder blades," "performing a lat pull down with the bar" to engage the lats, "driving the chest up to meet the bar," keeping "triceps to lats" or "elbows straight forward," and "driving feet through the floor" for a strong finish.12

name: Standing Barbell Overhead Press
description: Also known as the Strict Press or Military Press, the standing barbell overhead press is a vertical pressing movement that primarily engages the anterior and medial deltoids (shoulders), upper trapezius (traps), and triceps. It involves pressing a barbell directly overhead from a standing position, demanding significant upper body strength and core stability.32
progressions: The primary progression is to increase the weight. The Paused Overhead Press is a variation that can also increase difficulty by enhancing time under tension.32
regressions: Alternatives for developing overhead pressing strength include the Seated Dumbbell Press or using a Machine Shoulder Press
which can offer more support or reduce spinal loading.25
contraindications: Common mistakes to avoid include using the legs to assist the press (which turns it into a push press)
pressing the bar forward instead of directly overhead
and attempting to move the feet to re-rack the bar before safely lowering it.32
cues: Key cues include "bracing the abs tight" to maintain a neutral back, avoiding pausing at the bottom after the first repetition to utilize stretch reflex, "aiming for your nose on the way up and down" to keep the bar path efficient, and "reaching as high as you can" to ensure full lockout. Other cues include "tucking the ribs into the belly button," "squeezing the glutes," and "pressing straight up and together" while bringing the "bicep to the ear".32

name: Lat Pulldown
description: The lat pulldown is a vertical pulling movement performed on a cable machine, specifically designed to target the latissimus dorsi (lats), which are the largest muscles in the upper body. It also strengthens the teres major, lower and mid trapezius, rhomboids, posterior deltoids, and biceps. This exercise mimics the pulling mechanics of a pull-up but offers adjustable resistance, making it accessible for beginners and a versatile tool for advanced lifters to develop back width and strength.34
progressions: Increasing the resistance is the primary progression. Variations like narrow or underhand grips can shift emphasis to the biceps or lower lats. Single-arm pulldowns improve unilateral strength
and kneeling pulldowns engage the core more aggressively.34
regressions: Beginners can start with lighter weights or resistance bands. The straight-arm pulldown isolates the lats with minimal bicep involvement
serving as a good preparatory exercise.34
contraindications: Common mistakes to avoid include excessively arching the back
using momentum instead of controlled movement
pulling the bar down too far (which can stress the shoulder joint)
and not controlling the eccentric (negative) phase of the movement
as these can reduce muscle activation and increase injury risk.34
cues: Sit comfortably with feet flat and upper thighs tucked under the pad. Grasp the bar with a wide, overhand grip. "Pull from your armpits" to activate the lats, bringing the bar to chin level. "Squeeze shoulder blades together" and "keep chest up, core tight, and shoulders down and back." Drive elbows toward the ribcage. Pause and squeeze at the bottom, then control the bar's gradual ascent.34

name: Leg Press
description: The leg press is a resistance training exercise performed by pushing the legs against a weighted platform. It is highly effective for building leg strength and increasing muscle mass, primarily targeting the quadriceps and glutes. The design of the machine allows for adjustable foot placement, which can help isolate specific muscles like the hamstrings or glutes, making it valuable for addressing muscle imbalances or weaknesses.36
progressions: The primary progression involves increasing the weight on the platform. Single-leg press variations can also be used to increase difficulty and address unilateral strength.36
regressions: Reducing the weight is the most direct regression. Limiting the range of motion can also make the exercise more accessible for beginners or those with mobility limitations.37
contraindications: Common mistakes include allowing the knees to collapse inwards (indicating weak glutes)
locking out the knees at the top of the movement (which shifts tension to the joints and can cause strain)
and allowing the heels to hang off the foot pad or lift during the press (which places undue strain on the knees and reduces muscle activation).36
cues: Position feet hip-width apart so knees form 90-degree angles. Grip the handles, "keep your back and head against the pad," and "keep your core engaged." Lower the platform by slowly bending the knees (inhaling), then push the weight back up by extending the legs (exhaling). Focus on "equal weight in the big toe, pinky toe, and heel" and "spreading the feet apart" or "driving the knees to the shoulders".36

name: Single-Arm Dumbbell Row
description: The single-arm dumbbell row is a unilateral exercise performed by holding a dumbbell in one hand while supporting the body with the opposite hand and knee on a bench. This movement effectively targets the upper back muscles, including the latissimus dorsi, rhomboids, and trapezius, as well as the biceps. It is valuable for improving unilateral strength, addressing muscular imbalances, and enhancing core stability.19
progressions: Increasing the weight of the dumbbell is a direct progression. More advanced variations include the Renegade Row (performed from a plank position
demanding greater core stability) and the Single-Arm Anti-Rotational Row.19
regressions: using a lighter weight or reducing the range of motion can make the exercise more manageable. A supported standing row can also be used as a preparatory movement.38
contraindications: It is important to avoid torso rotation
excessive arching of the lower back
or shrugging the shoulders during the lift
as these can compromise form and increase injury risk.38
cues: Begin by holding a dumbbell in one hand and placing the opposite knee and hand on a bench. "Contract your abdominal/core muscles" to stiffen the torso and stabilize the spine, maintaining a "flat back" and "head aligned with your spine." "Depress and retract your scapulae" (pull shoulders down and back). Extend the arm holding the dumbbell towards the floor without allowing the torso to rotate. "Pull the dumbbell upwards, bending your elbow and pulling your upper arm backwards," keeping the arm close to the side of the body.38

name: Downward-Facing Dog (Adho Mukha Svanasana)
description: One of the most recognizable and popular yoga poses, Downward-Facing Dog forms an inverted V-shape with the body. It effectively stretches the hips, hamstrings, and calves while simultaneously strengthening the ankles, quadriceps, and shoulders. This pose also tones the abdominal muscles, decompresses the spinal column, and can help alleviate fatigue.10
progressions: Advanced variations include performing the pose on one leg with the opposite arm extended. Other related poses like Dolphin Pose and Puppy Pose can also serve as progressions.10
regressions: dropping to the knees (Tabletop position) can make the pose more accessible. Hands can be placed wider or fingers angled out for tight shoulders. Bending the knees or widening the legs can accommodate tight hamstrings
and using forearms or a wedge-shaped block can alleviate wrist sensitivity.10
contraindications: Individuals with carpal tunnel syndrome or arthritis
or those in late-term pregnancy should avoid or modify this pose.10
cues: "Spread your fingers" and "root the index finger and thumb." "Press down and forward through the knuckles" and "rotate your biceps forward." "Squeeze your elbows toward each other" and "lift the inner armpit." "Root your shoulder blades against your back ribs" and "draw your belly button in towards your spine." "Firm your quadriceps" and "press your heels toward the floor." "Relax your neck" and "lift up through sits bones," "drawing thighs toward the back wall" and "shifting weight back into hips".10

name: Warrior I (Virabhadrasana I)
description: Warrior I is a powerful standing yoga pose that simultaneously strengthens and stretches various parts of the body. It builds strength in the legs, buttocks (glutes), hip flexors, and shins, while stretching the hamstrings, calves, and ankles. The pose also lengthens the psoas and stretches the upper body and arms, contributing to power in the back and improving balance and focus.6
progressions: one can touch the palms overhead
or gently arch the spine backward. More advanced variations involve bringing the front palm flat on the floor or aiming for the front thigh to be parallel to the floor.6
regressions: Beginners or those with limitations can take a shorter stance or keep feet hip-distance apart for increased stability. Practicing Warrior I seated in a chair or placing hands on hips or the chair for support can also make it more accessible. For shoulder discomfort
bending elbows into a "Cactus pose" can relieve strain. Raising the back heel on a sandbag can help with back heel grounding.6
contraindications: This pose should be avoided or modified by individuals with leg
or high blood pressure. Those who tend to easily lose balance should use support.6
cues: "Align the front knee over the ankle" and "anchor the outer edge of the back foot to the ground." "Draw the shoulders down" and "tuck the tailbone under." Engage the muscles on the outer side of the bent knee to prevent it from drifting inward. "Lift your front hip points" to maintain an upright pelvis. "Press evenly through the center of your front heel and the outer edge of your back foot." "Reach through your fingertips".6

name: Child's Pose (Balasana)
description: Child's Pose is a deeply restorative yoga posture often used as a resting pose within a sequence or for calming the body before or after practice. It effectively releases tension in the low back, shoulders, and neck, while lengthening and stretching the spine. This pose also calms the central nervous system, stretches the hips, knees, thighs, and ankles, and gently massages the internal organs. It is known for its ability to reduce stress, fatigue, headaches, and insomnia.42
progressions: engages and stretches the back muscles and shoulders more actively. Coming up on tented fingertips can deepen the stretch.45
regressions: a blanket can be placed beneath the sitting bones if sitting on heels is uncomfortable
or under the forehead if it doesn't reach the floor. Spreading the knees wide or extending the arms behind with palms up can also modify the pose for different body types or to relax shoulders.44
contraindications: or ear/eye infections should exercise caution. Pregnant individuals should raise their head and chest with a bolster. Those with low back pathologies may find relief by using a bolster under the knees.44
cues: "Kneel down and touch your big toes together, then lower your hips back to sit on your heels." "Fold forward, resting your torso over your thighs (or between them if knees are wide)." "Extend your arms in front (palms down) or back (palms up)." "Rest your forehead on the mat." "Lengthen and widen the spine with each inhale," and "sink deeper into the pose with each exhale." "Keep the arms engaged by reaching through the hands," "sink down into the hips," and "relax the shoulders down, away from the ears." "Allow the body to dissolve into the mat," "notice the points of pressure," and "let go of any tension".44

name: Cat-Cow Pose (Marjaryasana-Bitilasana)
description: Cat-Cow is a gentle, flowing sequence between two poses that serves as an excellent warm-up for the spine, increasing its mobility and relieving tension in the upper body, including the back, shoulders, and neck. In Cat Pose (Marjaryasana), the spine is rounded on an exhale, drawing the abdomen in. In Cow Pose (Bitilasana), the lower back is curved, and the head and sternum are lifted on an inhale.42
progressions: As the spine becomes more accustomed to bending
one can explore deeper movements. The Cat-Cow flow can also be performed in standing or seated variations.49
regressions: A slower pace and focusing on a smaller range of motion can make the movement more accessible for beginners or those with limited mobility.49
contraindications: should avoid or modify this pose.49
cues: Begin in a Tabletop position with "hips directly over your knees" and "hands slightly ahead of your shoulders." For Cow Pose, "inhale and arch your back by lowering your belly, lifting your chin and sternum, and broadening your collarbones." For Cat Pose, "exhale and bring your abdomen in, arching your spine and bringing your head and pelvis down." "Move with your breath," initiating the movement "from your hips, not your neck." "Keep the back of your neck long" and "your core slightly toned".42

name: Mountain Pose (Tadasana)
description: Often regarded as the "mother of all yoga poses," Mountain Pose is a foundational standing posture that appears simple but demands significant awareness and balance. It effectively decompresses the spine, strengthens the entire leg and pelvic girdle, and tones the abdominal muscles. Regular practice contributes to improved posture and ignites the nervous system.42
progressions: practicing against a wall can be beneficial. Using a yoga strap looped around the shins to push out against it can activate the abductors (outer hips). Squeezing a block between the inner thighs can activate the adductors (inner thighs).51
regressions: standing with feet hip-width apart can provide a wider base of support.50
contraindications: or high blood pressure should approach this pose with caution.50
cues: "Stand straight with feet hip-width apart or together." "Spread all 10 toes" and "find equal weight in the four corners of your feet." "Firm your quadriceps" and "slightly rotate the inner thighs backward." To engage the core, "lengthen your tailbone" and "draw your pubic bone up," as you "draw your hip points in toward your navel." "Breathe into your back body" and "lift your sternum." "Root your shoulder blades against your back ribs" and "lift through the crown of your head," softening your gaze. "Draw your lower ribs back" if they tend to jut forward.50

name: Tree Pose (Vrksasana)
description: Tree Pose is a balancing posture that cultivates a sense of groundedness through the strength of the standing leg while simultaneously teaching the ability to reach tall. It tones leg muscles, engages core muscles, enhances balancing abilities, and aids in spinal alignment. This pose builds confidence and improves posture, fostering continuous engagement of ankles, legs, and core to maintain equilibrium.52
progressions: Progressions involve moving the hands from heart center to extending the arms overhead
symbolizing "growing branches." Advanced variations include Standing Lotus or single-leg knee tucks (from a plank
regressions: one can use a "kickstand" position with toes on the mat or practice while standing a few inches from a wall. Placing the ankle on the opposite shin while seated in a chair
or simply keeping hands on the hips
can also make the pose more accessible.52
contraindications: or ankle pain/sensitivity should exercise caution. If lifting arms causes shoulder pain
cues: "Shift your weight to one foot" and "find your drishti" (a steady gazing spot). "Place your foot somewhere along your inner leg line, avoiding the knee." "Direct your bent knee behind you to open your hips." "Maintain a slight bend in your standing leg." "Keep your weight in the center of your foot" and "engage your core to protect your low back and maintain spinal length." "Lift your chest" and "draw your shoulder blades down your back".52

name: Corpse Pose (Savasana)
description: Corpse Pose, also known as Savasana, is a restorative yoga posture typically performed at the conclusion of a yoga session. The practitioner lies face up with legs comfortably spread and arms relaxed alongside the body. This pose is crucial for recovering from the physical and mental challenges of a yoga sequence, allowing the body to relax deeply and prepare for meditation. It promotes overall relaxation, calms the nervous system and mind, and can alleviate stress, fatigue, headaches, and insomnia, while also contributing to lower blood pressure.42
progressions: The progression in Savasana is often internal
and preparing for meditation through specific breathing techniques or guided visualization.46
regressions: a bolster can be placed under the knees to relieve low back tension or pain. For pregnant individuals
raising the head and chest with a bolster or folded blankets is recommended. An eye pillow can also be used to block out light and deepen focus.46
contraindications: Individuals with low back pathologies may experience pain when lying flat and should utilize support under the knees. Pregnant women require elevation of the head and chest. Those with severe ear or eye infections should exercise caution.46
cues: "Gently recline onto your back and extend your legs." "Release your legs, soften the groin, and let your feet turn out evenly and naturally." "Position your lower back by lifting your pelvis, pressing it toward your tailbone, and then resting it back onto the mat." "Allow your arms to settle alongside the body, palms facing upward to open the chest." "Close your eyes and take a deep inhale." "Scan your body for any residual tension and breathe into that space." "Allow the body to dissolve into the mat, feeling it sink heavily into your space." "Notice the points of pressure along the backside of the body," and "let go of any tension that may be residing in the body".46

name: Power Clean
description: The Power Clean is an Olympic lift that involves lifting a barbell from the floor to the shoulders in one explosive, dynamic movement. It emphasizes speed and quickness, primarily developing explosive power, strength, and coordination throughout the legs, hips, and upper body. This lift is a cornerstone for enhancing overall athleticism and agility.14
progressions: The ultimate progression is the Full Power Clean

which combines all elements from the floor to the receiving position. Increasing the weight lifted is a continuous progression. Other advanced variations include the Hang Power Clean (performed from above or below the knees) and the Knee Pause Power Clean
which focuses on specific phases of the lift.14
regressions: To build up to the Power Clean
individuals can start with a Muscle Clean from the Hip
focusing on the hip extension and elbow wrap. Mastering the Front Squat is also crucial to ensure a correct receiving position. Lighter weights are essential for technique development.14
contraindications: It is critical to avoid rounding the low back or excessive hyperextension of the low back if the torso becomes too erect
as these can significantly increase the risk of injury. Loss of control during the lowering phase should also be prevented.56
cues: Begin with "feet shoulder-width apart" and "toes slightly turned out." Utilize a "hookgrip" for a secure hold. Position the "bar approximately 1 inch in front of the shins." Initiate the lift by "forcefully extending the hips and knees," ensuring the "torso angle remains constant." Keep the "shoulders over or slightly ahead of the bar" and the "bar close to the shins/thighs." Rapidly "shrug the shoulders" and "pull the body under the bar," catching it at the "anterior deltoids and clavicles" in a quarter-squat position.14
equipment: Weight Plates (bumper plates recommended for controlled drops).56

name: Power Snatch
description: The Power Snatch is a highly technical Olympic lift, similar to the Power Clean but distinguished by a considerably wider grip and a final bar position overhead. It is a dynamic movement executed from the floor to overhead in one continuous motion. This exercise develops explosive power, speed, and technical proficiency, demanding significant mobility through the hips, ankles, shoulders, and mid-to-upper back.54
progressions: Increasing the weight is the primary progression. Variations like the Hang Power Snatch (from various positions like above or below the knee) and the Dip Power Snatch are used to refine specific phases of the lift and enhance rate of force development.58
regressions: Preparatory exercises include the Muscle Snatch
which focuses on the pull and turnover without a squat
and Hang Snatch variations from higher positions (e.g.
upper thigh) to simplify the initial pull.58
contraindications: Significant mobility limitations in the hips
or mid-to-upper back can impede proper execution and increase injury risk. Poor body awareness and incorrect form
particularly allowing the bar to drift too far from the body
can lead to negative training effects.54
cues: "Squat down with hips lower than shoulders" and "grasp the bar evenly with a wide pronated grip." Position the "bar approximately 1 inch in front of the shins." "Forcefully extend the hips and knees," ensuring these joints extend at the same rate. "Keep the torso angle constant" and "shoulders over or slightly ahead of the bar." "Rapidly shrug the shoulders" and "pull the body under the bar," catching it "over and slightly behind the ears with fully extended elbows" in a quarter-squat position.57

name: Romanian Deadlift (RDL)
description: The Romanian Deadlift (RDL) is a deadlift variation that emphasizes a hip hinge movement with minimal knee bend, primarily focusing on strengthening the posterior chain muscles. This includes the hamstrings, glutes, and erector spinae. The RDL is crucial for developing powerful hip extension and establishing correct body positioning, which is a requirement for optimal alignment during other major lifts like the conventional deadlift.30
progressions: The primary progression is to increase the weight lifted. Single-leg RDLs are an advanced progression that further challenges balance and unilateral strength.9
regressions: For those new to the movement or with limited hamstring flexibility
starting with lighter weights is advisable. Good Mornings can also be used as a primary movement to reinforce the hip hinge pattern before progressing to the RDL.9
contraindications: It is essential to maintain proper posture throughout the movement. Avoid overarching or slouching the spine
allowing the shoulders to round forward
as these can lead to injury
cues: "Stand with your feet hip to shoulder-width apart" and position the "barbell over the midfoot." "Draw in and brace the abs," "lock the shoulder blades back and down," and maintain a "neutral spine." "Drive the hips back," keeping the "shins as vertically as possible." "Unlock the knees" slightly and "reverse the pattern, driving the hips back" to lower the bar only as far as good posture can be maintained and the hamstrings are at full length.30

name: Standing Hamstring Stretch
description: The standing hamstring stretch is a simple and effective way to target the hamstring muscles (biceps femoris, semitendinosus, and semimembranosus) located on the back of the thigh. These muscles are crucial for knee bending and hip extension. This stretch also indirectly engages the calves, adductors (inner thigh muscles), erector spinae (muscles along the spine), and glutes, helping to relieve tension in the legs, hips, and back.15
progressions: the individual can move their chest farther toward the floor.15
regressions: limit how far the chest moves toward the floor.15
contraindications: Individuals with acute hamstring injuries or significant lower back pain should exercise caution
especially if the stretch exacerbates discomfort.15
cues: "Stand with feet closer than shoulder-width." "Step forward with your left foot" and "flex the left foot up towards you." "Bend at the hips and place your hands on your thigh." "Keep the left leg straight as you slightly bend the right knee." "Feel the stretch along your left hamstring".62

name: Lying Quadriceps Stretch
description: The lying quadriceps stretch is performed while lying on one side or face down, by grasping the foot and pulling the heel towards the glute. This action effectively stretches the quadriceps (thigh) muscles, improving flexibility and range of motion in the knee and hip joints.63
progressions: one can point the knee behind the body while continuing to hold the foot. Another option is to hold the stretch for 10-15 seconds
then push the foot into the hand for 5-7 seconds
regressions: A reduced pull on the foot or less knee bend can make the stretch more gentle.
contraindications: Individuals with acute knee injuries or hip pain should avoid this stretch or perform it with extreme caution.63
cues: "Lie on your right side on a mat/floor with your legs extended." "Bend your left knee and pull your left heel up towards your left glute muscle," using your left hand to grasp the top of your left foot. "Keep your hips and shoulders aligned vertically to the floor" and "your head aligned with your spine." "Stiffen your core and abdominal muscles" to stabilize the spine and pelvis. "Gently pull your left heel and lower leg towards your tailbone" while keeping the "left thigh and knee resting on the inside of the right thigh".63

name: Standing Calf Stretch
description: The standing calf stretch is a two-part flexibility exercise designed to target both heads of the calf muscle: the gastrocnemius (stretched with a straight back leg) and the soleus (stretched with a slightly bent back knee). It is typically performed facing a wall, stepping back with one leg, and leaning forward to feel the stretch through the calf.65
progressions: one can bring the body closer to the wall
increase the bend in the front knee
or slightly flex the back knee to specifically target the soleus.65
regressions: Less lean towards the wall or a smaller bend in the front knee can reduce the intensity of the stretch.
contraindications: Individuals with acute calf injuries or Achilles tendon issues should avoid this stretch or seek professional guidance.65
cues: "Stand facing a wall, arms length away, with feet hip-width apart." "Extend your arms to place your palms on the wall." "Brace your core" and "depress and retract your scapulae." "Step back with your right leg into a split-stance position," keeping "both feet flat on the floor" and "toes pointing forward." "Increase the flexion (bend) in your left (front) knee" while "keeping the opposite leg straightened and pushing the heel into the floor".65

name: Overhead Triceps Stretch
description: The overhead triceps stretch is a simple flexibility exercise that targets the triceps muscles (on the back of the upper arm) and the shoulders. It is performed by extending one arm overhead, bending the elbow to allow the hand to drop to the middle of the back, and then using the other hand to gently apply pressure to the elbow to deepen the stretch.67
progressions: controlled pressure to the elbow with the opposing hand can deepen the stretch.67
regressions: Reducing the pressure applied or limiting the range of motion can make the stretch more comfortable.
contraindications: Individuals with acute shoulder injuries or elbow pain should avoid this stretch or perform it with extreme caution and professional guidance.67
cues: "Stand with feet hip-width apart" and "roll your shoulders down and back." "Reach your right arm to the ceiling," keeping the shoulder down. "Bending at the elbow, let your right hand drop to the middle of your back, palm facing your back." "Reach your left hand to the ceiling and place your fingers on your right arm, just above the elbow, applying light pressure to deepen the stretch".67

name: Doorway Chest Stretch
description: The doorway chest stretch is a flexibility exercise performed in an open doorway, designed to alleviate tension and improve flexibility in the chest (pectoralis major and minor) and shoulders. It involves placing the forearms on the doorframe and gently leaning forward through the doorway.69 This stretch is particularly beneficial for individuals who spend long hours at a desk, weightlifters, or those with tight muscles due to poor posture or repetitive activities, as it helps counteract hunching and improve spinal alignment.70
progressions: one can slowly step forward with one foot through the doorway or increase the lean.69
regressions: If the stretch is too intense
the elbows can be moved down slightly
or the lean can be reduced.69
contraindications: Individuals should avoid excessively arching the lower back. Those with existing shoulder injuries or intense neck pain should consult a professional
as this stretch could exacerbate certain conditions.70
cues: "Stand in a doorway with your elbows bent at shoulder height and your forearms resting on the doorframe." "Keeping your forearms and palms flat on the doorframe, gently lean through the doorway." "Keep your chest up and your head facing forward." "Ensure both arms are at right angles with your palms facing forward." "Avoid using jerky or sudden movements" and "maintain a rhythmic breathing pattern".69

name: Figure Four Stretch
description: The figure four stretch is a versatile flexibility exercise performed either lying on the back or seated. It involves crossing one ankle over the opposite knee and gently pulling the leg toward the chest. This stretch is highly effective for easing tightness and tension in the hips and lower back, specifically targeting the glutes (particularly the gluteus medius) and the piriformis muscle. It can significantly help in relieving back pain and improving sciatica symptoms by increasing mobility in the hip joints.16
progressions: one can use one hand to gently apply additional pressure to the raised knee as it is pulled toward the chest.16
regressions: after placing the ankle on the opposite knee
the heel can be slid closer to the butt while the foot remains on the floor
reducing the intensity of the pull.16
contraindications: Individuals with acute hip or knee injuries
or severe sciatica that is aggravated by the stretch
should avoid or modify this exercise.16
cues: "Lie on your back (or sit) with your knees bent and feet flat on the floor." "Bend one leg and place your ankle on your opposite knee." "Grasp the back of your thigh or the front of your knee (of the leg on the floor) and gently pull your knee toward you." "Feel a stretch in your hip muscles and the back of your leg".16

name: Seated Spinal Twist
description: The seated spinal twist is a yoga posture that involves rotating the upper torso, providing numerous benefits for spinal health and internal organs. It stimulates abdominal organs (including the liver and kidneys), lengthens the spine, stretches the outer hips, and opens the shoulders. This twist helps maintain optimal spinal health and can relieve mild backache and hip pain.72
progressions: one can interlace the hands for a bind or focus on twisting more deeply with each exhalation.73
regressions: one can simply hug the thigh. If there is low back or hip discomfort
extending the bottom leg can alleviate strain.73
contraindications: or shoulder pain should approach this pose with caution or modify it as needed.73
cues: "From a seated position, take your right foot up and over to your left, so your foot is pressing down on the outside of your left thigh." "Take your right fingertips behind you with palms or fingertips on the mat (or a block) to help keep your spine lifting and upright." "Inhale, press your hips down to lengthen your heart and entire spine upwards and lift your left arm up." "Exhale, hook your left elbow to the outside of your right thigh." "With each inhale, lengthen your spine more, and with each exhale, twist more deeply." "Keep your ribcage lifted and heart open," and "the gaze follows the spine as it twists open".73

name: Sun Salutation A (Surya Namaskar A)
description: A foundational flow comprising Mountain Pose, Raised Hands Pose, Forward Fold, Flat Back, Plank, Chaturanga Dandasana, Upward Facing Dog, and Downward Facing Dog.
progressions: Jumping back from Forward Fold to Plank or directly into Chaturanga.
regressions: For Chaturanga, use knees-down modification or practice against a wall.

cues.Raised Hands Pose: Lift arms overhead, palms touch or shoulder-distance apart.
cues.Forward Fold: Shift weight slightly into balls of feet, hips over ankles, relax neck.
cues.Flat Back: Lift head for natural spine extension, gaze few feet forward.
cues.Plank: Hands shoulder-distance, shoulders over wrists, wrap triceps back (elbows face back), squeeze hands slightly for chest engagement, press inner hands, scapular protraction (separate shoulder blades, lift heart), squeeze inner thighs, tuck tailbone, engage core, gaze down/slightly forward.
cues.Chaturanga Dandasana: Shift forward onto tippy-toes (shoulders past wrists), bend elbows straight back (hug ribs), lower until shoulders/upper arms parallel to elbows (not below), gaze down, neck long.
cues.Upward Facing Dog: Hands under elbows, squeeze elbows, draw shoulders back, press tops of feet, curl chest up, straighten arms, lift thighs off ground, activate legs, engage glutes, squeeze inner thighs, pull shoulder blades together, elevate through crown of head (lengthen neck), gaze forward.
cues.Downward Facing Dog: Lift hips, return to balls of feet, press back.

name: Sun Salutation B (Surya Namaskar B)
description: Builds upon Sun Salutation A by incorporating Chair Pose and Warrior I, adding more intensity and leg work.
progressions: Hold Chair Pose/Warrior I for longer durations.
Add arm variations in Chair Pose.

cues.Chair Pose (Utkatasana): Feet hip-width apart, sink hips low (as if sitting in a chair), arms overhead, engage core, 'tuck tailbone' slightly, draw ribs down.
cues.Warrior I (Virabhadrasana I): Front knee stacked over ankle, back foot angled about 45 degrees, hips squared forward, arms overhead, engage core, lift through chest.
cues.All other poses: Apply same precise cues as in Sun Salutation A.

name: Supine Lat Stretch Screen
description: Lying on your back with knees to chest (to flatten lumbar spine), arms extended overhead with palms up. Assess ability to bring arms to floor.
progressions: Actively press arms down to floor if possible (active stretch).
regressions: Perform with straighter legs if knees to chest is too restrictive.
Focus on gentle breathing to encourage relaxation.
cues: Lie flat on your back, press lower back into floor (knees to chest helps).
Arms straight overhead, palms facing up.
Gently try to bring arms to the floor.
Observe if arms 'dangle' or touch the floor.

name: Wall Angel Screen
description: Stand with back, head, and entire back against a wall. Arms in an 'L' shape (football goal post), elbows bent, forearms against wall. Slide arms up while maintaining contact.
progressions: Increase duration of hold at top.
Add light resistance band around wrists to maintain elbow width.
regressions: Feet further from wall to reduce lumbar arch compensation.
Focus on lower back contact first, then arms.
cues: Back, head, and entire back flat against the wall.
Arms in an 'L' shape (90-degree bend at elbows).
Attempt to flatten back of arms and hands against the wall.
Slide arms up, maintaining contact, without moving head or lower back.

name: Wall Ankle Mobility Test (Ankle Dorsiflexion Test)
description: Kneel with one foot 5 inches from a wall. Push knee directly over middle toe towards the wall while keeping the heel on the floor.
regressions: Start with foot closer to the wall (e.g., 3 inches).
cues: One foot 5 inches (handprint + thumb) from the wall.
Keep heel firmly on the floor.
Push knee directly over the middle toe towards the wall.
Observe if knee touches wall without heel lifting.

name: Thomas Test (Hip Internal/External Rotation Test)
description: Sit on the edge of a bed/bench with hips at the edge. Pull one knee to chest while allowing the other leg to relax. Assess position of relaxed leg.
progressions: Focus on actively relaxing the tested leg.
regressions: Don't pull knee quite as close to chest.
cues: Sit on edge of bed/bench, hips at edge.
Grab one knee, pull it to chest.
Gently fall backward onto your back.
Allow the opposite leg to relax completely.
Observe if relaxed leg lifts off bed or bends.

name: Flexion Intolerance Test
description: Observe if pain is exacerbated by actions such as sitting slouched, pulling up on the underside of a chair, bending movements like picking up objects from the ground, or deadlifting.
progressions: Gradually introduce light loads with perfect hip hinge mechanics.
cues: Consciously adopt positions that typically cause pain.
Note the exact trigger and pain intensity.
Compare pain levels with spine-neutral positions.

name: Extension Intolerance Test
description: Observe if pain is provoked by positions such as lying on the stomach, arching backward, or adopting an anterior pelvic tilt.
progressions: Gradually introduce gentle extension movements with controlled core bracing.
regressions: Focus on 'ribs down' cue in daily activities.
cues: Consciously adopt positions that typically cause pain.
Note the exact trigger and pain intensity.
Compare pain levels with spine-neutral positions.

name: Dynamic Loading/Instability Test
description: Observe if pain occurs with dynamic loading (running, jumping, Olympic lifts), or subtle micro-movements like sneezing/rolling over. A diagnostic test involves rising onto the toes and quickly dropping onto the heels.
progressions: Gradually reintroduce dynamic movements with strong core bracing.
regressions: Avoid dynamic loading; focus on static core bracing.
cues: Perform dynamic movements or controlled drop test.
Observe if pain is triggered by shockwave of load or micro-movements.
Note the exact trigger and pain intensity.

name: Load Intolerance Test
description: Observe if pain is triggered by holding a light weight at arm's length while taking deep breaths.
progressions: Gradually introduce light loads with strong abdominal bracing.
regressions: Seek assistance for daily lifting tasks.
cues: Hold a light weight at arm's length.

name: Proper Hip Hinging (Corrective Strategy)
description: Learning and consistently applying the movement pattern where the hips initiate the bend, keeping the spine neutral, as seen in movements like the 'short-stop squat' or 'golfer's lift.'
regressions: Wall hinge drill (touching butt to wall)
Downgrade with PVC pipe along spine.
cues: Maintain a long, neutral spine (avoid rounding or excessive arching).
Slight bend in knees, but focus on hip movement.

name: Ribs Down (Corrective Cue/Strategy)
description: A fundamental cue to prevent excessive spinal extension by engaging the core and drawing the lower ribs down towards the pelvis, maintaining a braced neutral spine.
progressions: Apply cue during all lifts (squats, presses).
Combine with Valsalva maneuver for maximal bracing.
regressions: Practice in supine (lying on back) with knees bent, pressing lower back into floor.
cues: Imagine pulling your lower ribs towards your belt line.
Avoid arching your lower back excessively.

name: Abdominal Bracing (Corrective Strategy)
description: A technique to increase intra-abdominal pressure by engaging the entire core musculature, providing stability to the spine for lifting and injury prevention.
progressions: Apply bracing to progressively heavier lifts.
Combine with Valsalva maneuver (holding breath with braced core).
regressions: Practice 'bracing for a punch' while lying on back.
Focus on 360-degree bracing, not just 'sucking in'.
cues: Imagine bracing for a punch to the stomach (tighten all around).
Breathe into your belly and sides, not just chest.

name: Handstand Preparation Drills (various)
description: A series of progressive drills to build strength, alignment, and body awareness for handstands. Includes Downward Dog hops, hollow body holds, Plank variations, and wall walks.
progressions: Progress from wall-assisted handstands to freestanding attempts.
regressions: Start with shorter holds for hollow body and planks.
Practice wall walks with feet lower on the wall.
Focus on smaller hops in Downward Dog.
cues: Look between hands or slightly forward (not directly up or down).

name: Crow Pose (Bakasana) Drills
description: Preparatory drills for Crow Pose, starting from a squat, placing knees on triceps, and gradually shifting weight forward into fingertips before lifting heels.
progressions: Transition from Crow Pose to other arm balances (e.g., tripod headstand).
regressions: Practice with blocks under feet or head for support.
Focus on weight shift without lifting feet initially.
Use a bolster or pillow in front for safety.
cues: Start in a squat, hands shoulder-width apart, fingers spread.
Place knees high on triceps (as close to armpits as possible).
Look forward, shift weight forward into fingertips.
Engage core, lift one heel, then the other, towards glutes.

name: Plank Variations (with Scapular Protraction)
description: Various plank positions (forearm plank, high plank) emphasizing active scapular protraction and core engagement.
cues: Shoulders directly over wrists (high plank) or elbows (forearm plank).
Push the floor away, protracting shoulder blades ('separate them,' 'lift heart').
Draw ribs and navel in, maintaining a straight line from head to heels.

name: Chaturanga Dandasana Modifications
description: Progressive modifications for Chaturanga, focusing on proper alignment and muscle engagement.
progressions: Hold at the bottom parallel position for longer.
regressions: Practice against a wall (standing push-ups at an angle).
cues: Start in Plank, shift forward onto tippy-toes (shoulders past wrists).
Hug elbows tightly to sides (like 'robot arms').
Lower until shoulders and upper arms are parallel to elbows (no deeper).
Maintain engaged core and long neck, gaze slightly forward.

name: Sama Vritti (Equal Ratio Breathing)
description: Breathing technique where inhalation and exhalation are equal in duration and intensity (e.g., 4-count inhale, 4-count exhale).
progressions: Practice in challenging poses to maintain calm.
cues: Inhale slowly through the nose for a count.
Exhale slowly through the nose for the same count.
Keep breath smooth and even, without strain.
Focus on the sensation of the breath.

name: The 4-7-8 Breath
description: A calming breath technique: Inhale for 4 counts, hold for 7 counts, exhale for 8 counts.
progressions: Integrate before sleep for improved rest.
regressions: Start with shorter counts, maintaining the 1:2 exhale ratio.
Practice in a relaxed, seated position.
cues: Inhale quietly through the nose for a count of 4.
Hold the breath for a count of 7.
Exhale completely through the mouth, making a 'whoosh' sound, for a count of 8.

name: Spinal Waves
description: A method for mobilizing, integrating, and articulating each individual section of the spine one at a time. Can be sagittal (forward/backward) or lateral (side-to-side).
progressions: Increasing fluidity, speed, and control through full range.
More complex variations or combining with other movements.
regressions: Potentially with external support or visual cues to isolate segments.
Focus on quality over speed initially.
cues: Move at each section individually one at a time.
Pretend that there's a wall in front... and behind you (for lateral waves).

name: Quadrupedal Movement (QM) / Locomotion (e.g., Lizard Crawl)
description: Ground-based bodyweight exercises using four points of contact (hands and feet), including crawling, sprawling, twisting/turning, reaching, and flowing. Lizard Crawl is a low-to-ground pattern with shoulders, torso, and hips hovering 1-2 inches above the floor, involving coordinated limb movement.
progressions: Increase distance/time (15-20ft, 30-40s continuous, up to 5 min for advanced).
regressions: For Lizard Crawl: two hands in contact while practicing hip ROM/foot placement; stationary reaching with lead arm.
Easier variations of specific QM patterns (e.g., simpler crawls, shorter distances).
cues: Keep the spine parallel to the floor.
Avoid excessive movement through the torso.
Imagine balancing a glass of water on your back. Don't spill a drop.
For Lizard Crawl, bend knee and internally rotate hip to stay lower.

name: Handstand Basics (Wall Handstand, Free Handstand)
description: Mastering the fundamental skill of balancing inverted on one's hands. Progresses from wall-supported variations to freestanding holds.
regressions: Crow Pose/Frog Stand (forearm support, foundational balance).
Pike Handstand against wall (feet on wall, hips stacked).
Back to wall handstand (facing wall, hands close).
Stomach to wall handstand (facing away from wall, controlled entry/exit).
cues: Head neutral or slight gaze forward.
Use fingers/wrists to control balance (like grabbing a ball).

name: Copenhagen Plank (Adductor/Groin Strength)
description: A challenging side plank variation specifically designed to strengthen the adductor muscles (inner thigh) and improve groin stability. Performed by supporting the body on one forearm and the top leg, with the bottom leg hanging or placed on a bench/elevated surface.
progressions: Top foot only on bench, bottom leg hanging freely.
Dynamic variations (e.g., lifting bottom leg to meet top leg).
regressions: Both knees bent, supporting body with top knee on bench.
Bottom knee bent, top leg extended on bench.
Regular side plank with leg lift.
cues: Maintain a straight line from head to heels.
Engage your core to prevent hip sag.
Actively squeeze the inner thigh of the top leg into the bench/support.
Control the movement, don't just hang.

name: Hanging Protocols (Passive & Active Hanging)
description: Series of exercises involving hanging from a bar to decompress the spine, strengthen grip, and improve shoulder health. Includes passive (relaxed) and active (shoulders engaged, scapular retraction/depression) variations.
progressions: Longer passive hangs (up to several minutes).
Active hangs (pulling shoulders down/away from ears).
regressions: Feet supported on a box (less bodyweight).
One-arm assisted hang (using other hand for support).
Shorter durations or more frequent breaks.
cues: For passive: fully relax shoulders, let gravity stretch.
For active: pull shoulder blades down and back, engage lats.
Breathe deeply and relax the rest of the body.

name: ATG Split Squat
description: A deep lunge variation where the front knee tracks significantly over the toes, often with the back heel elevated, to build full knee flexion strength and hip flexor flexibility.
regressions: Using support (e.g., holding onto a post)
cues: Keep the back leg straight and actively engaged (quads locked).
Allow front knee to track far over toes.
Aim for 'ass to grass' depth if possible.

name: Tibialis Raise
description: An exercise targeting the tibialis anterior muscle on the front of the shin, crucial for ankle dorsiflexion and knee deceleration.
progressions: Using a KOTG Tib Bar or dumbbell on toes
cues: Lift toes and ball of foot as high as possible.
Focus on the contraction of the shin muscle.

name: KOTG Calf Stretch / Elephant Walk
description: A dynamic stretch for the calves and hamstrings, emphasizing full ankle dorsiflexion and plantarflexion.
progressions: Deeper stretch (e.g., elevated surface for KOTG Calf Stretch)
Increased speed of movement in Elephant Walk
cues: Keep legs straight (or slightly bent for less hamstring pull).
Push heels towards the ground (in KOTG Calf Stretch).
Alternate driving heels down and lifting high (in Elephant Walk).
Feel the stretch in the calves and Achilles.

name: Reverse Nordic
description: An eccentric-focused exercise for the quadriceps, where the body leans back from the knees with the torso and hips in a straight line.
progressions: Holding a weight (e.g., medicine ball to chest)
regressions: Assisted (e.g., using a band, holding a pole)
Reduced range of motion (less lean back)
cues: Keep a straight line from knees to shoulders (avoid breaking at the hips).
Squeeze glutes to maintain hip extension.
Engage quadriceps to control the movement.

name: Sissy Squat
description: A quadriceps-dominant exercise where the body leans back from the knees, emphasizing extreme knee flexion and quad contraction.
progressions: Adding external weight (e.g., holding a plate)
cues: Keep a straight line from knees to shoulders.
Allow knees to track far over toes.
Lift heels high off the ground (on toes).

name: Patrick Step
description: An exercise where one steps down from an elevated surface, maintaining an upright torso, to load the VMO and inner quad through terminal knee extension.
cues: Keep the heel of the standing leg on the step.
Knee tracks forward over the toes as you step down.
Control the movement, don't just drop.
Feel the engagement in the inner quad just above the knee.

name: Seated Goodmornings
description: A hip hinge exercise performed seated with legs straight, focusing on hamstring length and spinal flexion/extension.
progressions: Adding external weight (e.g., barbell on back, dumbbell held to chest)
Increasing depth while maintaining straight legs
cues: Hinge from the hips, not the lower back (initially focus on keeping back flat, then allow controlled rounding as per KOTG's methods for spinal health).
Feel the stretch in the hamstrings.
Control the movement both down and up.

name: Hip Flexor Swimmers
description: A dynamic movement to improve hip flexor mobility and control, involving controlled leg swings or rotations.
progressions: Integrating into more complex movement flows
cues: Control the movement throughout the entire range.
Keep the rest of the body stable.
Focus on isolating the movement to the hip joint.

name: Friction Training (e.g., Backward Sled Pull)
description: Resistance training involving backward movement, often using a sled or similar friction device, for low-impact strengthening.
cues: Drive through the balls of the feet.
Focus on pushing the ground away.

name: Kettlebell Swing (Russian)
description: A powerful, ballistic hip-hinge movement where the kettlebell swings to chest height. Focuses on hip drive.
regressions: Focus on hinge mechanics without explosion
cues: Hinge, not squat (push hips back, slight knee bend).
Pack the shoulders (keep shoulders down and back).
Bell floats to chest height, not pulled with arms.

name: Kettlebell Swing (American)
description: A ballistic hip-hinge movement similar to the Russian swing, but the kettlebell travels overhead.
cues: Hinge, snap, punch overhead (controlled overhead extension).
Keep arms long (don't pull with shoulders).
Full lockout at the top (hips, knees, shoulders in line).

name: Goblet Squat
description: A fundamental squat variation holding a kettlebell against the chest, emphasizing proper squat mechanics and core stability.
progressions: Moving to double kettlebell front squat
cues: Elbows inside knees (at the bottom of the squat).

name: Kettlebell Clean & Press
description: A complex two-part movement: cleaning the kettlebell to the rack position (chest/shoulder) and then pressing it overhead.
cues: Absorb the bell softly (catch in the rack position).
Breathe behind the shield (core bracing for the press).

name: Kettlebell Snatch
description: A ballistic movement that transitions the kettlebell from the floor or hang to an overhead lockout in one fluid motion.
cues: Fast hands (quick transition through the handle).
Punch through the bell (strong lockout overhead).
Don't let the bell flop (control descent).

name: Turkish Get-Up
description: A complex, multi-planar movement that transitions from lying on your back to standing, holding a kettlebell overhead.
progressions: Increased fluidity and speed (while maintaining control)
cues: Eyes on the bell (maintain gaze on kettlebell overhead).
Each step is a strong position.

name: Farmer's Carry
description: Walking with heavy kettlebells (or dumbbells) in each hand.
progressions: Uneven carries (different weights in each hand)

name: Kettlebell Thruster
description: A compound movement combining a Goblet Squat with an overhead press, performed in a fluid motion.
regressions: Separate Goblet Squat and Overhead Press
cues: Use the legs to drive the press (generate momentum from the lower body).

name: Kettlebell Renegade Row
description: Performed from a plank position with hands on kettlebells, alternately rowing one kettlebell up to the side of the chest.
cues: Pull elbow to ceiling (drive with the back muscles).

name: Kettlebell Windmill
description: A complex movement involving a hip hinge and spinal rotation, often with a kettlebell pressed overhead, to improve oblique strength, shoulder stability, and hamstring flexibility.
cues: Keep eyes on the bell (overhead hand).
Straight leg, hinge at hip (rotate and push hips out).

name: Pancake Stretch (with PAILs/RAILs)
description: A seated stretch with legs spread wide, focusing on hip flexion and hamstring/adductor extensibility. Enhanced with isometric contractions.
progressions: Reduced reliance on external load (active control)
cues: Hinge from the hips, maintaining a flat back.
Actively engage quads to press knees down (extend legs).
For PAILs: Push heels/legs into floor (5-10s, 25-50% effort).
For RAILs: Actively pull torso deeper with hip flexors/core (5-10s).
Breathe deeply and relax into the stretch after contractions.

name: Jefferson Curl
description: A rounded spine forward fold designed to progressively lengthen the hamstrings and strengthen the spine in flexion.
progressions: Increasing height of platform (to go deeper)
Slower tempo, longer holds at bottom (PNF)
cues: Start by tucking the chin to the chest.
Slowly roll down, one vertebra at a time, allowing the spine to round.
Keep legs relatively straight but allow a micro-bend in knees if needed.
Focus on reaching towards the floor, not just hinging.
Control the eccentric phase and the return.

name: Cossack Squat
description: A deep side-lunge movement that challenges hip adductor and hamstring flexibility and strength at end range.
progressions: Adding external weight (e.g., kettlebell goblet style)
Moving to floor for a full middle split progression
cues: Keep the heel of the squatting leg on the ground.
Straight leg remains straight, foot ideally flexed.
Squat down as deep as possible with control.
Actively push the knee out on the bent leg.

name: Shoulder External Rotation (Loaded/Active)
description: Drills focused on improving the range of motion and strength in external rotation of the shoulder joint.
progressions: Adding light external load (e.g., small dumbbell, band)
Increasing time under tension at end range
Integrating into overhead pressing or handbalancing warm-ups
cues: Isolate movement to the shoulder joint, avoid compensation from torso.
Actively pull into the external rotation.

name: Spinal Segmentation Drills (e.g., Cat-Cow variations)
description: Exercises focusing on articulating individual vertebrae of the spine, promoting isolated movement and control.
progressions: Increased range of motion and isolation
Integrating into more complex movements (e.g., wave movements, flowing sequences)
regressions: Focusing on only one segment (e.g., thoracic)
cues: Move one vertebra at a time, like a ripple.
Avoid global movement; focus on isolation.
Breathe with the movement, exhaling on flexion, inhaling on extension.

name: Push-up Variations
description: A foundational bodyweight exercise for upper body pushing strength, scaled from beginner to advanced levels. Emphasizes clean form and control.
cues: Twist hands into the ground (for ring push-ups) to enhance stability.
Maintain clean form through full range of motion.

name: Dips
description: A critical bodyweight exercise for developing pushing strength, lockout strength, and stability, particularly in the triceps and shoulders.
cues: Shoulders remain nicely fixed locked into their joints.
Go only as deep as comfortable with good form.

name: Pull-up Variations
description: Fundamental vertical pulling patterns to build strength and mass in the back and biceps, with variations for different skill levels.
cues: Clean, controlled movement through the full range of motion.
(Implicit: focus on back and bicep engagement).

name: L-sit
description: A foundational exercise for developing core compression and straight arm strength, where the body is held in an 'L' shape off the ground.
cues: Tuck knees to chest for tuck L-sit.

name: Pancake Stretch
description: A deep seated hamstring and hip flexibility stretch, vital for improving external hip rotation and hamstring length.
progressions: Weighted Pancake (e.g., 10 reps with 10s hold on last rep)
cues: Keep hips connected to the surface.
Actively use own strength to get more flexible (engage quadriceps and hip flexors).

name: Bridge (Wheel Pose)
description: A movement to develop shoulder and spine flexibility, focusing on a deep backbend.
regressions: Easier variations with shorter range of motion or less arch
cues: Butt tight, belly tight (to protect lower back).

name: Wrist Warm-ups
description: A series of exercises designed to strengthen wrists, prevent injury, and enhance range of motion, crucial for handstands and other calisthenics.
regressions: Fewer repetitions, less aggressive range of motion
cues: Roll onto thumb (for wrist roller deviation).
Emphasize length around the wrist joint.

name: Shoulder Warm-ups
description: Routines designed to improve shoulder mobility, stability, and range of motion, essential for all upper body and hand balancing movements.
progressions: Loaded Shoulder Stretches (adjusting hand width, adding contractions)
regressions: Using lighter resistance or bodyweight only
cues: Push shoulder into ground (for wall chest stretches).
Reach hands backwards (retract shoulder blades) or pull hands down (contract bicep/pec) for loaded stretches.

name: Handstand (Basics & Progressions)
description: Developing the fundamental skill of balancing inverted on one's hands, progressing from wall-supported to freestanding holds and advanced shapes.
cues: (Implicit: Hollow body, active shoulders, straight arms, stacked joints)
